items.title: Relembre a palestra: O sistema você implanta, a mudança você constrói #SITCWB2026
items.author: AdrianoCWB
items.text:
No dia 7 de novembro, no Auditório Gregor Mendel da PUCPR, Jean Henrique Machado, Founder da JEMOW, apresentou no SAP Inside Track Curitiba 2026 a palestra "Gestão de mudança como competência organizacional (O sistema você implanta, a mudança você constrói)". 
 O vão da adoção 
 Jean abriu com uma ideia simples: o go-live é o começo da mudança, não o fim. A curva técnica (desenho, desenvolvimento, entrega) chega pronta ao go-live, mas a curva humana (envolvimento, adoção, uso) não, porque gente não muda na velocidade de um cronograma. O espaço entre as duas é onde o benefício do projeto se perde. 
 Por que o ritmo importa 
 Segundo a Accenture, o ritmo das mudanças que afetam as empresas aumentou 183% entre 2019 e 2023, e 75% dos líderes admitem que a capacitação das equipes não acompanha as mudanças impulsionadas por IA. Para o Brasil, ele lembrou que em 2027 a mesma pessoa vai absorver a reforma tributária (CBS no lugar de PIS e Cofins) e a nova jornada de trabalho, ao mesmo tempo. 
 Também citou que, segundo a APA, quem passa por mudanças recentes tem 2,5 vezes mais estresse prolongado e 3 vezes mais intenção de buscar outro emprego. 
 Não é resistência, é falta de energia 
 Pesquisa da Gartner citada na palestra mostra que a disposição dos colaboradores em apoiar mudanças caiu de 74% para 43% enquanto as mudanças por pessoa foram de 2 para 10 por ano. Muitas vezes o que chamamos de resistência é exaustão. 
 E quando há resistência de fato, ninguém resiste ao novo, resiste ao que perde. Jean usou o modelo SCARF, de David Rock: status, certeza, autonomia, pertencimento e justiça. 
 Como aplicar na prática 
 Defina o sucesso em comportamento antes do go-live: expectativa, materialização e sustentação. 
 Prepare o gestor direto: ele é o canal número 1 da mudança, entre quem decide e quem usa. 
 Meça adoção por velocidade, utilização plena, proficiência e sustentação. Se você não mede adoção, você mede esperança. 
 Passe de projeto para competência: usuário treinado vira pessoa capaz, go-live realizado vira adoção real. 
 Para levar 
 Antes de perguntar como vencer a resistência, pergunte o que a pessoa está perdendo. 
 Mudança não desce pela hierarquia por gravidade. 
 Se a mudança agora é contínua, gestão de mudança tem que ser uma competência permanente da organização. 
 Sobre o palestrante 
 Jean Henrique Machado, Founder da JEMOW, com 18 anos em desenvolvimento humano e 5 em gestão de mudança. 
 Assista à palestra no YouTube: https://youtu.be/VOQZl1Tc6Hw 
 Veja todas as palestras no post índice: https://community.sap.com/t5/curitiba-blog-posts/sap-inside-track-curitiba-2026-relembre-as-palestras-sitcwb/ba-p/14522453

items.title: From Pipeline to Proposal: How AI Powers the Opportunity-to-Quote Stage in SAP
items.author: Parisa_Mahdavi
items.text:
The gap between identifying an opportunity and delivering a compelling quote is where deals are won or lost. Sales representatives need to know which deals are worth pursuing, what to say when they get in the room, and how to guide buyers to the right products quickly. SAP Sales Cloud Version 2 and SAP Commerce Cloud address each of these challenges through a set of AI capabilities that work across the entire Opportunity-to-Quote stage. 
 This post walks through each capability — what it does, how it works, and the business value it delivers. 
 SAP Sales Cloud Version 2 — Smarter Selling at Every Step 
 Predictive Opportunity Scoring — Focus on the Deals That Will Actually Close 
 Pipeline inflation is one of the most persistent problems in B2B sales. Only around 40% of forecasted opportunities are actually closed — meaning sales teams routinely spend time and resources on deals that will not convert. Without a reliable signal to separate high-probability deals from low-probability ones, prioritization becomes guesswork. 
 Predictive Opportunity Scoring , delivered through Deal Intelligence in SAP Sales Cloud Version 2, solves this by assigning each opportunity a data-driven win score — updated daily — giving sales representatives and managers a consistent, objective basis for prioritization. 
 How It Works 
 The feature uses machine learning trained on your organization's historical opportunity data. The model identifies patterns from past won and lost deals and applies them to active opportunities to generate a unique win score per opportunity. Sales representatives can hover over the score to see the top influential factors — the specific attributes that most impacted the score, such as deal size, sales stage, or engagement level. 
 Two Model Options 
 SAP Sales Cloud Version 2 offers two model options to accommodate different levels of data maturity: 
 Model How It Works Key Factors Available? 
 Native Model Trained on your own historical data ✅ Yes 
 SAP-RPT Model Foundation model — no training data required ❌ Win score only 
 The SAP-RPT Model (Relational Pretrained Transformer) is particularly valuable for new implementations or organizations with limited historical datasets. However, it is not available by default — customers must raise a support case via the CEC-CRM-ML component to gain access. 
 Business Text Intelligence — Never Miss a Critical Follow-Up 
 Sales representatives capture a great deal of important information in free-text notes — customer commitments, next steps, follow-up requests. In practice, these notes are often reviewed once and then forgotten. 
 Business Text Intelligence uses Natural Language Understanding (NLU) to read these notes and automatically surface appointment recommendations, ensuring that critical next steps are acted on rather than overlooked. 
 For example, a note reading "Customer asked us to follow up next week with a revised proposal" would trigger a recommended action to schedule a follow-up appointment — directly within the opportunity or lead record. 
 Beyond its standalone value, Business Text Intelligence is a required prerequisite for enabling Post-Meeting Brief . Administrators must activate the NLP Classification, Business Text Intelligence, and Business Entity Recognition models before Post-Meeting Brief can be configured. 
 Pre-Meeting Brief — Walk Into Every Meeting Fully Prepared 
 Preparation time before a customer meeting is limited. Sales representatives often need to search across multiple records — opportunities, cases, previous emails, interaction histories — to get a complete picture before they walk into a conversation. The Pre-Meeting Brief eliminates that effort. 
 Available in the General tab of Appointments and Visits, the Pre-Meeting Brief automatically aggregates the following context in a single view: 
 Deal and Lead Updates — recent changes to linked transactions, so there are no surprises during the meeting 
 Past Interaction Insights — a summarized history of previous customer interactions, including sentiment analysis, providing context on the relationship tone 
 Account Insights — third-party buying intent signals from Bombora , helping sellers align their conversation with what the customer is actively researching 
 Critical Cases — open support issues from SAP Service Cloud Version 2, so sellers are aware of active customer concerns before the conversation begins 
 Pending Recommended Actions — outstanding actions identified by Business Text Intelligence from previous notes, ensuring commitments made in past interactions are visible and followed up 
 Post-Meeting Brief — Turn Every Conversation Into Actionable Intelligence 
 While the Pre-Meeting Brief prepares sellers before a conversation, the Post-Meeting Brief captures what happened during it. 
 The Post-Meeting Brief becomes available only after an appointment is marked as Completed and was conducted via Microsoft Teams . Rather than pulling from existing CRM data, it analyzes the actual meeting transcript to generate its insights, surfacing: 
 An overview with sentiment analysis of the conversation 
 Attendees, topics, and keywords extracted from the discussion 
 Recommended actions such as follow-up tasks or meetings 
 These recommended actions feed directly back into the Pre-Meeting Brief of the next appointment with the same customer — appearing as Pending Recommended Actions and ensuring continuity across the entire sales engagement cycle. 
 Intelligent Selling Services — Real-Time Personalization That Starts Immediately 
 Unlike static, rules-based recommendation engines, ISS operates as a real-time personalization platform that learns and adapts with every customer interaction. Personalization begins immediately — even for first-time visitors — and becomes increasingly precise as the system gathers more behavioral signals. 
 The engine continuously optimizes for two goals simultaneously: customer relevance and business impact . This dual optimization distinguishes ISS from simpler recommendation tools. 
 ISS delivers recommendations tailored to every stage of the customer journey: 
 Trending Products and Personalized Products — engage customers from the first click, based on real-time activity and browse history 
 Complementary Products and Replenishment Products — draw on completed order data to identify what customers buy together and when they are likely to re-purchase 
 Recently Viewed Products and Related Products — help customers rediscover or explore alternatives to products they are already considering 
 Related Products — Crowd Behavior That Works From Session One 
 The Related Products feature surfaces alternative products linked to the item a customer is currently viewing — driven by crowd behavior analysis rather than manual product linking or category rules. 
 The underlying model uses collaborative filtering at the crowd level : it analyzes what other customers viewed when interacting with the same product, then predicts the current user's next likely click and surfaces those products accordingly. 
 Because it draws on collective behavior rather than individual history, it is effective even for anonymous or first-time visitors — a significant advantage in both B2B and B2C commerce scenarios. It is one of the most immediately deployable recommendation types, working from session one with no prior user data required. 
 Complementary Products — What Goes Together 
 The Complementary Products feature analyzes past purchase transactions to identify which products are most frequently bought together. This is a basket analysis model anchored to completed orders , not browsing behavior — making it more accurate than view-based association. 
 Recommendations appear on the Product Page and Cart Page — two high-intent moments when surfacing the right complementary item increases average order value and helps the customer complete their purchase. 
 Replenishment Products — The Right Product at the Right Time 
 The Replenishment Products feature goes a step further by incorporating time as a key variable . Using deep learning on historical transaction data, the model learns not just what a customer buys, but when they are likely to need it again. 
 The system applies intelligent suppression — withholding a recommendation until the timing is appropriate, so the experience feels natural rather than intrusive. For example, if a customer buys a particular product once a week, the recommendation appears only after a few days have passed since their last order containing that product. 
 Replenishment recommendations appear on the Order Details and Order List pages — meeting customers at the moment they are reviewing past purchases, which is particularly effective in B2B scenarios where repeat procurement is common. 
 The feature directly supports three measurable business outcomes: 
 Customer Lifetime Value — through ongoing repeat purchases 
 Customer Retention Rate — through timely, relevant prompts 
 Repeat Customer Rate — by reducing friction in the re-purchase journey 
 SAP Commerce Cloud AI — Summary 
 Capability Core Technology Primary Business Outcome 
 Product Recommendations (ISS) Real-time ML personalization Improve product discovery and drive conversion 
 Related Products Crowd-level collaborative filtering Reduce browse abandonment, surface relevant alternatives 
 Replenishment Products Deep learning with temporal analysis Increase repeat purchase rate and customer retention 
 The Bigger Picture 
 In the Opportunity-to-Quote stage, every minute a seller spends searching for context, chasing notes, or waiting for a buyer to find the right product is a minute the deal is not progressing. The capabilities covered here directly reduce that friction: 
 SAP Sales Cloud Version 2 ensures sellers know which opportunities to prioritize, what to follow up on, and how to show up to every conversation prepared. SAP Commerce Cloud ensures buyers find the right products quickly — transforming the storefront from a passive catalog into an active, intelligent selling tool that shortens the path from product discovery to quote request. 
 Together, they create a connected, AI-powered layer across one of the most critical stages in the Lead-to-Cash journey.

items.title: AI Agents in Action: How SAP CX AI Toolkit Powers the Quote-to-Order Stage
items.author: Parisa_Mahdavi
items.text:
The Quote-to-Order stage is where customer intent becomes a transaction — and where service quality directly impacts conversion. Customers have questions about orders, delivery timelines, and product specifications. Cases arrive that need to be triaged, routed, and resolved. Knowledge gets captured in case notes and email threads that no one ever finds again. SAP addresses each of these challenges through four purpose-built AI agents, all built and managed within the SAP CX AI Toolkit . 
 This post walks through each agent — what it does, how it works, and the value it delivers at this critical stage of the sales cycle. 
 The Platform: SAP CX AI Toolkit 
 Before exploring the individual agents, it helps to understand where they live. All four agents are built and managed through the SAP CX AI Toolkit , a cloud-native platform that brings generative AI capabilities to SAP Customer Experience applications. 
 At its core is the AI Agent Builder , where administrators configure agent templates, define data sources and triggers, write instructions, and map outputs back to SAP Sales Cloud Version 2 records. Every agent follows the same pattern: listen for a trigger, process input using LLM models and configured enterprise data, write the result back into the relevant business object. 
 What makes this architecture particularly powerful is agent-to-agent collaboration . When a task falls outside one agent's scope, it transfers the conversation seamlessly to another agent better equipped to handle it. A Digital Service Agent handling an order cancellation request, for example, can hand off directly to an Order Processing Agent — with full context — so the right agent always handles the right task. 
 These handoffs are managed through a structured system using templates, priority queues, and routing logic, allowing a chain of agents to work together in an orchestrated manner — each contributing its specialized capability to resolve complex customer scenarios end-to-end. This autonomous execution is what distinguishes AI agents from traditional AI tools that require a user to initiate every action manually. 
 Q&A Agent — Immediate Answers From Enterprise Data 
 During the Quote-to-Order stage, customers regularly have questions: order status, delivery timelines, product specifications. Finding answers typically means searching through multiple systems or waiting for a human agent to research and respond. 
 The Q&A Agent eliminates that wait. When a question is submitted, the agent interprets the intent, searches the configured enterprise data sources — knowledge bases, historical tickets, case records — and returns a grounded answer with source references, automatically. 
 Administrators configure it through the AI Agent Builder by selecting the Q&A Agent template, defining which data sources to query, specifying the types of questions the agent should handle, and mapping the generated answer back to the relevant SAP Sales Cloud field. 
 The result is immediate, consistent responses without manual research — at the exact moment in the sales cycle when customers need fast, accurate answers to move forward with their order. 
 Prerequisites: The SAP CX AI Toolkit must be integrated with SAP Cloud for Customer or SAP Sales Cloud and SAP Service Cloud Version 2, and Intelligent Q&A access must be enabled for the relevant data sources before the agent can be created. 
 Service Classification Agent — Smarter Triage From the Moment a Case Arrives 
 When a customer submits a support case — by email, chat, or web form — someone needs to determine what the issue is, how urgent it is, and who should handle it. At high volumes, manual triage is slow and produces inconsistent results when different agents interpret similar cases differently. 
 The Service Classification Agent automates this process entirely. It reads the incoming case content, identifies issue type and priority using generative AI — not just keyword matching — and automatically updates category, priority, and team assignment fields. 
 Consider a practical example: a customer writes, "Our order from last week arrived with damaged packaging, and two items are missing." The agent analyzes the text, categorizes the case as a fulfillment and quality issue, sets the appropriate priority, and routes it to the logistics team — before a human agent has even seen it. 
 For order-related service requests, this speed matters. Fulfillment issues that sit unassigned while customers wait can escalate quickly. The Service Classification Agent applies the same classification logic to every incoming case, reducing the time between case creation and first response and ensuring consistent routing from the moment a case is created. 
 Digital Service Agent — Self-Service That Actually Resolves 
 Not every customer issue requires a human agent. Routine inquiries — warranty questions, troubleshooting steps, order status — can and should be resolved without creating a case at all. 
 The Digital Service Agent is a customer-facing AI that provides conversational self-service, drawing on business knowledge configured in the SAP CX AI Toolkit: FAQs, policy documents, product manuals, and support articles uploaded via Azure Blob Storage. For order-related inquiries such as order status checks, it can be combined with the Shopping Agent , which provides sub-agents for order status retrieval and other transactional capabilities. 
 When a question is too complex for self-service, the agent initiates a seamless handoff to a human agent in SAP Service Cloud Version 2 — transferring the full conversation context so the customer never has to repeat themselves. 
 The business case is straightforward: fewer routine cases reach the human service team, customers get immediate answers without waiting in a queue, and human agents can focus on complex cases that genuinely require human judgment and expertise. 
 How the Four Agents Work Together 
 Agent What It Does Key Integration 
 Q&A Agent Answers natural language questions from enterprise data Knowledge bases, cases, tickets 
 Service Classification Agent Classifies, prioritizes, and routes incoming cases automatically Service categories, team assignment 
 Digital Service Agent Provides conversational self-service with human handoff Customer-facing channels, knowledge base 
 Knowledge Base Article Generation Agent Generates draft articles from resolved cases Case notes, emails, interaction history 
 These four agents form a connected system. The Service Classification Agent ensures cases reach the right team. The Q&A Agent helps agents find answers quickly. The Digital Service Agent resolves routine issues before they become cases. The Knowledge Base Article Generation Agent captures solutions so they can be reused across all channels — including by the other agents. 
 The Bigger Picture 
 The Quote-to-Order stage demands speed, consistency, and accuracy. A delayed response to a case, an unanswered question, or a missed follow-up can slow or stop a transaction entirely. The four agents in the SAP CX AI Toolkit address each of these risks — not as isolated tools, but as a coordinated system that handles triage, self-service, knowledge retrieval, and documentation autonomously. 
 For organizations running SAP Customer Experience, this represents a meaningful shift: from AI that assists humans with individual tasks, to AI agents that execute multi-step workflows end-to-end — freeing human teams to focus on the interactions that genuinely require their expertise.

items.title: Closing the Loop: How AI Powers the Order-to-Cash Stage in SAP, Part 1
items.author: Parisa_Mahdavi
items.text:
SAP Cloud ERP — Automation and Intelligence Across the Sales Fulfillment Cycle 
 The Order-to-Cash stage is where sales execution meets operational reality. Orders need to be created accurately, fulfillment needs to be monitored, and issues need to be resolved before they escalate into customer problems. Part 1 of this series explores how SAP Cloud ERP embeds AI directly into the sales fulfillment cycle — automating data entry, scoring financial risk, and giving sales teams real-time visibility into every order through Joule. 
 Sales Order Automatic Completion — Eliminating the Data Entry Bottleneck 
 Incomplete sales orders are one of the most common sources of fulfillment delays. Missing fields slow down processing, trigger rejections, and require manual follow-up — consuming time that sales representatives could spend on higher-value activities. 
 Sales Order Automatic Completion removes this friction through AI-powered recommendations that fill in missing fields in real time. The system analyzes historical sales document item data from the past year, identifies patterns in customer-specific preferences, and intelligently predicts missing or incorrect details — not just filling gaps, but enriching the data with contextually accurate information. 
 The key benefits are concrete and measurable: 
 Intelligent Data Enrichment : Analyzes historical data to predict missing or incorrect details, ensuring completed orders are accurate and aligned with each customer's specific preferences. Accuracy improves as more data is processed. 
 Efficiency and Time Saving : Delivers a 25% reduction in manual effort by providing AI-powered recommendations for missing fields, freeing sales teams to focus on nurturing customer relationships and increasing productivity. 
 Reduction of Errors and Rejections : Minimizes order errors, reduces rejections, and eliminates the need for rework — saving time and resources. 
 Adaptability and Learning : The AI continuously learns from user interactions and evolving data, becoming increasingly accurate with every engagement. 
 AI-Assisted Behavioral Insights for Contract Accounting — Identifying Risk Before It Becomes a Problem 
 In accounts receivable and contract accounting, the ability to identify high-risk customers early — before outstanding balances escalate — is a significant operational advantage. Behavioral Insights for Contract Accounting delivers this through machine learning-powered risk scoring and predictive analysis. 
 The solution analyzes customer behavior across multiple scenarios to generate risk scores and insights, enabling financial users to identify high-risk accounts quickly, optimize collection strategies based on customer-specific behavioral patterns, and support proactive, data-driven decision-making to reduce outstanding debt. 
 This capability requires two solutions working together: 
 SAP Behavioral Insights — provides customer behavior analysis, risk scoring, and an expanded overview of events for efficient, reliable analysis 
 Intelligent Scenario Lifecycle Management (ISLM) — a self-service framework for managing the lifecycle of machine learning scenarios, from training models to generating inference results 
 Two Implementation Approaches 
 SAP Cloud ERP supports two approaches for deploying machine learning scenarios: 
 Approach Description Best For 
 Embedded ML tools run on the same system as SAP Cloud ERP; uses APL (for business analysts) and PAL (for data scientists) Organizations preferring tight integration 
 Side-by-Side SAP Cloud ERP and ML infrastructure run in separate stacks Organizations requiring flexibility, scalability, or external ML services 
 The business outcomes are measurable: reductions in days sales outstanding (DSO) , uncollectible accounts receivable write-offs, and customer billing, credit, and collections costs. 
 Sales Order Fulfillment Monitoring — Joule as Your Fulfillment Co-Pilot 
 Even well-entered orders can encounter blocking issues during fulfillment — credit holds, delivery blocks, billing problems, trade compliance flags. Finding and resolving these issues manually requires navigating multiple applications and cross-referencing documents. Joule , embedded directly within the SAP Cloud ERP environment, changes this. 
 Sales representatives can use Joule to check whether a sales order's fulfillment is on track, identify blocking issues across all fulfillment phases, and navigate directly to the relevant application to resolve them — all through natural language queries. 
 Joule analyzes and resolves fulfillment issues across four phases : 
 Order Processing 
 Incomplete Data : Identifies missing mandatory information at header and item levels, including item count 
 Credit Block : Highlights financial risks, displaying credit utilization, risk class, and credit limit details 
 Trade Compliance : Checks embargo status, legal control status, and screening status — only abnormal statuses are displayed 
 Supply Processing 
 Purchase & Quantity Confirmation : Tracks unconfirmed quantities and purchasing confirmation statuses (not confirmed or partially confirmed) 
 Delivery Processing 
 Delivery Block : Details specific block reasons, whether at header or item level, and the count of items affected 
 Delivery Creation : Flags items that are overdue or due later, indicating partial or no delivery 
 Billing 
 Billing Block : Lists block reasons and affected item counts that are preventing invoice generation 
 Beyond detecting issues, Joule summarizes findings, groups them into issue categories, provides concise diagnoses with handling suggestions, and routes users directly to the most relevant application view — eliminating manual app searches entirely. 
 Sales Order Status Check — Natural Language Transparency Across the Full Order Lifecycle 
 Sales teams need real-time visibility into order status without spending time navigating multiple systems. Joule's Sales Order Status Check delivers this through plain-English queries submitted directly within SAP Cloud ERP. 
 Sales representatives can ask about a specific order's status, and Joule detects issues such as incomplete data, delivery blocks, and billing blocks — summarizing findings, grouping them into issue categories, and providing handling suggestions. From each issue card, Joule routes directly to the most relevant application view, where users can edit the order, address missing fields, and remove blocks before saving changes to enable fulfillment. 
 This capability delivers measurable outcomes: faster, more intuitive resolution of sales order issues, improved staff productivity, and reduced customer cancellations due to delayed fulfillment. 

 The four SAP Cloud ERP capabilities covered in Part 1 address the Order-to-Cash stage from two directions: preventing problems before they occur (Automatic Completion, Behavioral Insights) and resolving them quickly when they do (Fulfillment Monitoring, Status Check with Joule). Together, they reduce manual effort, improve data accuracy, and keep the fulfillment cycle moving. 
 Part 2 covers how SAP Service Cloud Version 2 completes the picture — equipping service teams with the AI-powered context, knowledge retrieval, and summarization capabilities they need to handle every customer interaction with speed and precision.

items.title: Maintaining Classification Code Mapping in Core Data Management for Next Gen SAP Ariba Buying
items.author: DDINESH
items.text:
Introduction 
 Classification Code Mapping enables automatic material group determination in Next Gen SAP Ariba Buying. By mapping commodity codes to material groups, the system can automatically assign the correct material group when buyers select items from catalogs or create purchase requests. This guide explains what Classification Code Mapping is, why it's required, and provides a step-by-step walkthrough for uploading and configuring mappings using Core Data Management (CDM). 
 What is Classification Code Mapping? 
 Classification Code Mapping defines the relationship between commodity codes (classification codes) and material groups in your ERP system. This mapping entity allows SAP Ariba Buying to automatically determine the appropriate material group when a purchase request line item is created. 
 How Mapping Works 
 When a buyer selects an item with a commodity code, the system: 
 Looks for an exact match in the mapping table 
 If no exact match, traverses parent codes in the hierarchy until a match is found 
 If no hierarchical match, checks for wildcard pattern matches 
 If still no match, uses the default fallback (asterisk entry) 
 Mapping Types 

 Type 
 Example 
 Description 

 Exact 
 IT-HW-001 
 Maps a specific commodity code directly to a material group 

 Hierarchical 
 (automatic) 
 System traverses parent codes until a match is found 

 Wildcard 
 IT-HW* 
 Matches any code starting with the prefix 

 Default 
 * 
 Fallback when no other mapping matches (required) 
 Why is Classification Code Mapping Required? 

 Purpose 
 Benefit 

 Automatic Material Group Determination 
 Eliminates manual entry of material groups on purchase requests 

 ERP Integration 
 Ensures correct material group flows to SAP S/4HANA for posting 

 GL Account Assignment 
 Material group drives general ledger account determination 

 Data Consistency 
 Standardizes material group assignment across all procurement documents 

 Process Efficiency 
 Reduces errors and speeds up requisition creation 

 Compliance 
 Ensures proper categorization for spend reporting and audits 
 Key Configuration Points - Critical for Success 
 This section addresses the most common configuration mistakes that cause mappings to fail. Read this carefully before uploading any data. 
 To Source System - The #1 Cause of Mapping Failures 
 The To Source System value in your mapping MUST exactly match the Data Source value in the Product Group (Material Group) entity. 
 How to find your To Source System value: 
 Open Core Data Management 
 Navigate to Product Group (Material Group) entity 
 Look at the Data Source column 
 Copy this value EXACTLY - this is your To Source System 
 Example: 
 In Product Group entity: 
 ┌─────────────────┬─────────────┬──────────────┐ 
 │ Material Group │ Description │ Data Source │ 
 ├─────────────────┼─────────────┼──────────────┤ 
 │ L001 │ IT Hardware │ S4HC │ 
 │ L002 │ Software │ S4HC │ 
 │ A001 │ Services │ S4HC │ 
 └─────────────────┴─────────────┴──────────────┘ 

 Your To Source System = S4HC 
 What goes wrong with mismatched To Source System: 
 ❌ Mapping file has: To Source System = "ERP_SYSTEM" 
 Product Group has: Data Source = "S4HC" 
 Result: Material group NOT determined - system can't find the material group 

 ✅ Mapping file has: To Source System = "S4HC" 
 Product Group has: Data Source = "S4HC" 
 Result: Material group determined correctly 
 Domain Name Must Match Classification Codes 
 The From Domain in your mapping must EXACTLY match the Product Classification Domain in your classification codes: 

 If Classification Codes have 
 Then Mapping must have 

 Product Classification Domain = custom 
 From Domain = custom 

 Product Classification Domain = unspsc 
 From Domain = unspsc 

 Product Classification Domain = UNSPSC 
 From Domain = UNSPSC 
 Case sensitivity matters! custom ≠ Custom ≠ CUSTOM 
 Default Fallback Entry is REQUIRED 
 You MUST include an asterisk (*) entry as the default fallback. Without it, any commodity code that doesn't match will result in NO material group being assigned. 
 Example of required default entry: 

 From Source System 
 From Domain 
 From Version 
 From Classification 
 To Source System 
 To Domain 
 To Version 
 To Classification 

 COMMON 
 custom 
 0 
 ***** 
 S4HC 
 ProductGroup 
 L001 
 From Source System is Always "COMMON" 
 Unlike To Source System (which varies by ERP), the From Source System should always be COMMON for classification code mappings. 
 To Domain is Always "ProductGroup" 
 The To Domain field must always be ProductGroup (exactly as shown, with capital P and G). 
 How to Upload Classification Code Mapping 
 Data Preparation 
 Before uploading mappings, download the sample template from Core Data Management (CDM) by clicking Download Sample on the Product Classification Code Mapping entity. 
 Template Structure 
 The upload template contains one sheet: 

 Sheet 
 Purpose 

 ProductClassificationCodeMap 
 Mapping data between classification codes and material groups 
 Field Definitions 

 Field Name 
 Data Type 
 Mandatory 
 Description 

 From Source System 
 String 
 Yes 
 Always use "COMMON" 

 From Domain 
 String 
 Yes 
 Must match your classification code domain exactly 

 From Version 
 String 
 Yes 
 Must match your classification code version 

 From Classification 
 String 
 Yes 
 Commodity code, wildcard pattern, or * for default 

 To Source System 
 String 
 Yes 
 CRITICAL: Must match Data Source in Product Group entity 

 To Domain 
 String 
 Yes 
 Always use "ProductGroup" 

 To Version 
 String 
 No 
 Leave blank 

 To Classification 
 String 
 Yes 
 Material group code from your ERP system 
 Real Example: Filled Excel Template 
 Here's a complete example showing how to fill the mapping sheet. This example uses the custom classification codes from the Classification Codes blog. 
 Scenario: 
 Classification domain: custom 
 ERP System ID (Data Source): S4HC 
 Material Groups: L001 (General), L002 (IT Hardware), L003 (IT Software), A001 (Services) 
 ProductClassificationCodeMap Sheet 
 From Source System From Domain From Version From Classification To Source System To Domain To Version To Classification 
 COMMON custom 0 * S4HC ProductGroup L001 
 COMMON custom 0 IT-HW S4HC ProductGroup L002 
 COMMON custom 0 IT-HW-001 S4HC ProductGroup L002 
 COMMON custom 0 IT-HW-002 S4HC ProductGroup L002 
 COMMON custom 0 IT-HW-003 S4HC ProductGroup L002 
 COMMON custom 0 IT-SW* S4HC ProductGroup L003 
 COMMON custom 0 SVC S4HC ProductGroup A001 
 COMMON custom 0 SVC-001 S4HC ProductGroup A001 
 COMMON custom 0 SVC-002 S4HC ProductGroup A001 
 Key points in this example: 
 Row 1 (*) : Default fallback - any code without a specific mapping gets material group L001 
 Rows 2-5 (IT-HW...) : Exact mappings for IT Hardware codes → L002 
 Row 6 (IT-SW) *: Wildcard mapping - ALL codes starting with "IT-SW" → L003 (covers IT-SW-001, IT-SW-002, etc.) 
 Rows 7-9 (SVC...) : Exact mappings for Services codes → A001 
 Notice: 
 From Domain = custom matches the classification codes domain exactly 
 From Version = 0 matches the classification codes version exactly 
 To Source System = S4HC matches the Data Source in Product Group entity 
 To Domain = ProductGroup (always this value) 
 How This Example Resolves Material Groups 

 User Selects Code 
 Resolution Path 
 Material Group 

 IT-HW-001 
 Exact match found 
 L002 

 IT-HW-999 
 No exact match → parent IT-HW found 
 L002 

 IT-SW-001 
 Wildcard IT-SW* matches 
 L003 

 IT-SW-999 
 Wildcard IT-SW* matches 
 L003 

 SVC-001 
 Exact match found 
 A001 

 UNKNOWN 
 No match → default (*) 
 L001 
 Upload Procedure 
 Prerequisites 
 Configure required integration and assign necessary business roles, business catalogs, and user roles to manage data in the connected ERP system 
 Assign the user group "cap - Manager" which provides: 
 View-only access to the core data entities list and file upload logs 
 Upload access for all allowed entities 
 Download access for allowed 'common' entities 
 Ensure material groups are available in the Product Group (Material Group) entity 
 Upload classification codes to the Product Classification Codes entity first 
 Steps to Upload Classification Code Mapping 
 Identify Target ERP System ID 
 Open Core Data Management 
 Navigate to Product Group (Material Group) entity 
 Note the value in the Data Source column 
 This is your To Source System value - copy it exactly 
 Prepare Mapping Data 
 [ ] From Source System = COMMON (for all rows) 
 [ ] From Domain matches classification codes domain exactly 
 [ ] From Version matches classification codes version exactly 
 [ ] To Source System matches Data Source from Product Group entity 
 [ ] To Domain = ProductGroup (for all rows) 
 [ ] Default (*) entry exists 
 Download the sample template from the Product Classification Code Mapping entity 
 Fill in the mapping data using the example above as reference 
 Checklist before upload: 
 Access Core Data Management 
 Open the Master Data File Upload tile on the SAP Fiori launchpad 
 Upload Product Classification Code Mapping 
 Open the Product Classification Code Mapping entity 
 Upload the mapping file 
 Select Common as the business system ID in the Source System field 
 Review the uploaded information after completion 
 Verify Mappings 
 Check that all mappings are loaded correctly 
 Verify the default (*) entry exists 
 Confirm To Source System values match your ERP system 
 Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them 

 Mistake 
 Symptom 
 How to Fix 

 Wrong To Source System 
 Material group shows blank on PR 
 Get exact value from Product Group entity Data Source column 

 Case mismatch in From Domain 
 Mapping not found 
 Copy domain name from classification codes 

 Missing default (*) entry 
 Some PRs have no material group 
 Add a row with From Classification = * 

 To Domain spelled wrong 
 All mappings fail 
 Use exactly "ProductGroup" (capital P, capital G) 

 From Version doesn't match 
 Mapping not found 
 Match version from classification codes 

 Using ERP system name instead of ID 
 Mapping fails 
 Use technical ID (e.g., S4HC), not name 
 Troubleshooting Guide 
 Material Group Not Determined 
 Check in this order: 
 To Source System matches? 
 Open Product Group entity → Check Data Source column 
 Compare with To Source System in your mapping 
 Must be IDENTICAL 
 Domain matches? 
 Open Product Classification Code entity → Check domain value 
 Compare with From Domain in your mapping 
 Must be IDENTICAL (case-sensitive) 
 Version matches? 
 Compare From Version in mapping with Version in classification codes 
 Default entry exists? 
 Check mapping has a row with From Classification = * 
 Wrong Material Group Assigned 
 Check the mapping priority: 
 Exact match takes priority over wildcard 
 Wildcard takes priority over hierarchical 
 Hierarchical takes priority over default 
 If getting unexpected results, check for conflicting mappings. 
 Verification Checklist 
 After uploading, verify these items: 
 [ ] Mappings visible in Product Classification Code Mapping entity 
 [ ] To Source System matches Data Source in Product Group entity 
 [ ] From Domain matches classification codes domain 
 [ ] Default (*) entry exists 
 [ ] Create a test requisition and verify material group is auto-populated 
 [ ] Test with codes at different levels to verify hierarchy resolution 
 Demo Video: Click Here

items.author: BirgitOe
items.text:
When you post costs to an EPPM project with revenue in SAP S/4HANA Cloud, how does the system know which customer, product, and sales organization to put on that posting so it shows up correctly in margin reporting? The answer is attributed profitability segment derivation, and understanding it is the key to getting drillable margin reports from day one. 
 This blog explains how the derivation works for EPPM projects, why it is more complex than for CPM customer projects, and what determines your reporting quality in practice. It covers the Multiple Sales Order Items Scenario flag and the effect of its YES/NO setting on how characteristics are derived; the role of the project master profitability segment as the most reliable anchor regardless of your sales order structure; and how the substitution mechanism turns a labor-intensive multi-field manual entry into a single-field lookup. Making project master maintenance sustainable at scale. 
 We hope this blog helps you get the most out of profitability reporting and that you find at least one thing you can apply directly in your project. Happy reading! 
 Stefan Walz and Birgit Oettinger

items.title: Mastering CBAM Compliance: What SAP’s Latest Release Means for Declarants
items.author: Gunther Rothermel
items.text:
Under the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), importers of steel, aluminum, cement, fertilizers, electricity, and hydrogen into the EU now face direct legal and financial accountability for the embedded emissions in those products. 
 Calculate the cost of carbon emissions 

 Learn how 

 To help them manage it, the latest release of SAP Sustainability Footprint Management delivers a CBAM compliance engine for declarants, complemented by SAP Green Ledger for liability and asset management. 

 The urgency is concrete. Starting in February 2027, companies importing goods into the EU will need to buy CBAM certificates, with prices linked to the EU Emissions Trading System and currently ranging between €75 and €82 per ton of CO₂ . The first annual reporting deadline is September 30, 2027, covering all imports made since January 1, 2026. This means businesses have less than a year to ensure their often manual and fragmented compliance processes are ready. 

 In practical terms, carbon is now a priced input for importers, one that directly affects margins, cash flow, and sourcing decisions. The question is whether companies manage that exposure through scalable, auditable processes or continue piecing it together in spreadsheets. 

 Inside the October release 

 The October release of SAP Sustainability Footprint Management builds out the CBAM compliance and declaration workflow from raw import data to EU registry-ready output. 

 These existing apps in SAP Sustainability Footprint Management have been extended with CBAM capabilities: 

 Manage footprint inventory scope now supports adding and managing a dedicated CBAM scope. 

 Import master data extends to CBAM-relevant business objects, including business partner information tied to non-EU suppliers. 

 Manage location enables upload and management of supplier locations, a critical foundation for actual supplier emission factors. 

 Import business transactions introduces a new transaction type for customs import declarations, the foundational data that drives CBAM calculations. 

 To further streamline CBAM compliance, three new apps handle the core compliance workflow: 

 View default CBAM emission factors provides access to SAP-maintained content including the EU’s default emission factors, benchmarks, and markups that apply when supplier-specific data is not available. This matters financially. Default values carry a 10% markup in 2026, rising to 20% in 2027 and 30% from 2028. 

 Manage actual CBAM emission factors is where that penalty gets addressed. Declarants can upload supplier-provided emission factors and use them in place of defaults, directly reducing their certificate obligations and cost exposure. 

 Manage CBAM reports is the calculation and reporting engine. In a single run, it computes embedded emissions, certificates to surrender, and indicative cost based on date of import at scale. EU registry-ready CBAM declarations are generated instantly with full data traceability, documented calculations, and change logs to support auditability. 

 Beyond the core applications, the release includes built-in dashboards that surface emissions, certificate requirements, and cost exposure across suppliers and products. And the analytics layer gives companies visibility into where their embedded emissions sit. This intelligence supports not just compliance, but targeted supplier engagement and decarbonization strategy. 

 From emissions to the balance sheet 

 CBAM creates a new class of financial liability. Every ton of embedded CO₂ in imported goods translates into certificates that must be purchased and surrendered, priced weekly against the EU ETS auction rate. Under both IFRS and U.S. GAAP, provisions must be recognized now for the liabilities arising from CBAM obligations—covering reported emissions and the resulting requirement to surrender carbon certificates, even though cash doesn’t move until certificate purchases begin in February. 

 The recent integration between SAP Sustainability Footprint Management and SAP Green Ledger for CBAM connects the compliance engine to financial accounting. SAP Green Ledger manages the liability and certificate asset life cycle—from initial exposure recognition through settlement preparation—and creates the entry point for further financial process integration: liability forecasting, margin analysis and simulation, and product costing (planned for 2027). As CBAM expands to cover more products and free allowances phase out, the cost impact will grow. SAP Green Ledger gives finance teams the visibility to protect margins and steer business decisions. 

 SAP Sustainability Footprint Management quantifies the embedded emissions. SAP Green Ledger turns that into a number your CFO can act on. Together, these solutions help finance teams treat CBAM the same way they do any other managed obligation: planned, measured, settled. 

 What comes next 

 In Q1 2027, SAP Sustainability Footprint Management will source customs data directly from SAP Global Trade Services. File upload and API integration are already available now for sourcing customs data from SAP and non-SAP sources. 

 The broader CBAM picture only intensifies from here. Free allowances under the EU ETS, the mechanism that historically shielded European producers from the full cost of carbon, are being phased out between now and 2034. As those allowances decline, the effective cost of CBAM certificates rises will rise. Also, the scope of covered goods will expand with roughly 180 downstream steel and aluminium products in 2028, with glass, ceramics, chemicals, plastics, and oil refining expected after 2030. 

 Companies that build their compliance processes on scalable, auditable foundations now will be positioned to absorb those expansions. Companies that do not will find themselves re-engineering under pressure each time the scope widens. 

 CBAM is not a one-time filing. It compounds in cost and complexity each year. 

 SAP’s CBAM solution for declarants is available now. To learn more, visit the Sustainable Finance area of sap.com , explore what the CBAM definitive regime means for you, and calculate your CBAM costs using this calculator . 

 Gunther Rothermel is chief product officer for SAP Sustainability.

items.title: Building Your First Agentic Use Case: New Whitepaper Offers a Road Map for Enterprise AI
items.author: Tim Clark
items.text:
As enterprises accelerate their agentic AI investments, a significant question is emerging: Are they prepared to trust AI agents to make decisions and take actions on their behalf? 
 A cloud-native layer that unifies SAP and non-SAP data into trusted, multidomain views 

 Explore SAP Reltio 

 This was a major topic of discussion during Reltio’s inaugural Agentic Executive Leadership Program, which brought together 22 senior executives from different industries, including financial services, life sciences, manufacturing, and consumer goods, for three working sessions in October 2026. 

 The findings, detailed in a new whitepaper, Trusted Before Autonomous , suggest that the biggest obstacles to enterprise AI adoption involve the quality of the data, business context, governance, and the human oversight supporting it all. 

 Authored by Kash Mehdi, vice president and field CTO at Reltio, an SAP company, the whitepaper identifies four priorities for organizations seeking to move AI agents from experimentation into production. 

 Business context makes the difference 

 One of the program’s most revealing demonstrations illustrated how quickly business context can influence AI-generated results. 

 When a customer-success agent was asked to identify renewal accounts requiring attention, an agent operating with company-specific business definitions identified 13 accounts, complete with performance indicators and recommended actions. Without those definitions, the same question produced 23 accounts based on the agent’s own assumptions. The context-aware agent also consumed approximately 25% fewer tokens because it understood where to find relevant information. 

 For SAP customers managing complex enterprise environments, business information frequently spans ERP, CRM, service, and third-party systems. That’s why AI agents must understand the underlying data and the relationships, definitions, and business rules that give it meaning. 

 Another demonstration showed an agent assembling 35 entities and 55 relationships across multiple enterprise systems to develop recommendations ahead of an executive meeting. 

 It’s another reminder that access to enterprise data alone does not guarantee intelligent decision-making. Agents still need the context to interpret that information correctly. 

 Governance must precede autonomy 

 Even though enterprise leaders are eager to expand AI capabilities, the program revealed considerable caution about allowing agents to operate independently. 

 When asked what conditions must exist before an agent takes action, 69% of participants prioritized having a named human accountable for mistakes. An equal percentage emphasized establishing boundaries that agents cannot cross. Another 62% wanted organizations to define what constitutes an incorrect action before deployment. 

 It’s not hard to see why. An inaccurate report can be reviewed, challenged, or ignored. An autonomous agent, however, can execute an incorrect decision directly within a business workflow. 

 To address these risks, the whitepaper introduces a five-stage autonomy framework, progressing from observation and human-approved recommendations to limited autonomous actions and exception-based reporting. The framework recommends keeping high-consequence decisions under human approval while allowing greater autonomy for lower-risk, reversible activities. 

 Closing the gap between recommendations and results 

 Even when AI systems generate useful recommendations, organizations may struggle to translate them into measurable business outcomes. 

 An example involving a pharmaceutical company’s go-to-market operations underscore this struggle. Its AI system generated approximately 38,000 recommendations monthly, with reviewers rating 86% as good. Yet only five percent were executed, and outcomes were reported for just one percent. This disconnect highlights a roadblock that cannot be solved with more technology. 

 Organizations need employees who can evaluate recommendations, integrate them into existing workflows, monitor results, and intervene when necessary. Thankfully, the whitepaper identifies three essential organizational capabilities that can help: inquiry, oversight, and integration. 

 Together, these capabilities help employees determine whether AI is solving the right problem, recognize when intervention is required, and establish repeatable processes for turning recommendations into action. 

 Keeping enterprise context current 

 Another challenge is ensuring that the business context supporting AI remains accurate as organizations evolve. 

 One pharmaceutical executive described an environment containing 30 to 40 data lakes and a project involving 300 million documents. Given this environment, even simple questions about sales or customers can produce different answers depending on departmental definitions and underlying systems. Mergers, acquisitions, organizational changes, and evolving business rules introduce additional complexity. 

 The whitepaper recommends continuously gathering, governing, curating, distributing, and retiring business context so that AI agents operate with relevant, current information. 

 A practical road map for the first 100 days 

 Rather than encouraging organizations to pursue enterprise-wide autonomy immediately, the program outlines a measured 100-day implementation strategy: 

 The first 30 days focus on selecting a use case, establishing baseline performance, and assigning ownership. 

 The next 30 introduce controlled experimentation, human approvals, and tested safeguards. 

 Days 61 through 90 emphasize measuring outcomes against the original baseline, while the final phase documents lessons learned and determines whether the organization is ready to expand. 

 For SAP customers exploring agentic AI, the path to Autonomous Enterprise operations doesn’t begin with giving agents more freedom, but with establishing the trusted data, business context, governance, and human capabilities required to make that freedom productive.

With the release 2611 of SAP Digital Manufacturing, the Production Connector gains a capability that customers and partners have been eagerly awaiting: it can now act as an OPC UA Server. items.title: Retroactive billable maintenance in Service with Advanced Execution
items.author: Abhishek_Ramesh
items.text:
The Billable maintenance process always had a limitation, wherein the maintenance order can converted to a billable maintenance order only before the order has been released. Once the maintenance order is released, then there was no capability to convert the order or charge the costs in standard. 
 However, it is a very common situation in certain industries, that the decision to charge the cost is sometimes very late in the process. The execution of the maintenance work itself is mostly urgent. However, due to legal processes, insurance claims or simply because the decision requires a detailed inspection, sometimes the decision to charge a customer is made after the maintenance work has been completed. This capability was not at all available in the previous releases. This is resolved with the latest release of Service with Advanced Execution.

Mail receiver adapter

42.teaching_angle: Use it in a CPI troubleshooting session: trace where message processing time goes, then discuss timeout settings, retry behaviour and attachment size limits. Ask trainees to check the claim against the current adapter documentation before relying on it.

Auth type: OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion with principal propagation intended.

No resolution or accepted answer is included in the post.

37.why_it_matters: Principal propagation only works when the runtime has a user identity to pass along. Choosing between a user token and SystemUser also changes which identity SuccessFactors sees, which affects authorisation.

deep_dives.title: Designing a secure file download with RAP OData V4 and Edm.Stream
deep_dives.explanation:
The post (ref 32) describes serving AL11 application-server files through a RAP OData V4 service that returns content as Edm.Stream. Only the abstract is available, so the code below is my own sketch of the pattern and not taken from the post. It is meant for discussion.

In RAP, a stream is normally modelled as a media property: an `xstring` content field annotated with `@Semantics.largeObject` (mimeType, fileName, contentDispositionPreference), plus a MIME type field. Reading the file means `OPEN DATASET ... FOR INPUT IN BINARY MODE` on a path your code builds. That is where the security risk lies.

The controls the post lists map to concrete checks. First, never accept a path from the client. Accept a key such as a logical folder ID and a file name. Resolve the folder from a configuration table. Second, validate the file name against a whitelist (no `/`, `\`, `..`, or control characters), then check that the resolved path still begins with the mapped directory. Third, check the file size before reading into an `xstring`, because large files exhaust memory. Fourth, call the authorisation check before opening the file. The post says this check is replaceable, so it would sit behind an interface.

In the ABAP standard, logical file names (transaction FILE, `FILE_VALIDATE_NAME`) are the usual way to constrain paths. The post does not say whether it uses them, so ask this when reviewing. Also ask whether DCL or a behaviour-level authorisation covers the entity, or only a custom class does.
key_concepts: File size limits before xstring read

deep_dives.title: Principal propagation in BTP destinations: reading the OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion error
deep_dives.explanation:
The question (ref 37) reports the error 'Cannot determine user to propagate for OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion destination' from a BPA action calling SuccessFactors. The error text lists two remedies: provide a user_token JWT when retrieving the destination, or configure the destination with SystemUser.

With OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion, the destination service builds a SAML assertion for a specific user and exchanges it for a token at the target system. It needs a user identity as input. If the call comes from a runtime that has no user JWT, such as a process started in a technical context, the service cannot build the assertion.

The post does not give the root cause. My inference is that the workflow runs without the Work Zone user's token, but this is unconfirmed. To narrow it down, check whether the process is triggered with the user's context, and whether the BPA action receives a user token at all.

The two remedies differ in meaning. A user_token keeps the real user, so SuccessFactors applies that user's permissions. SystemUser maps every call to one configured identity, which is simpler but loses per-user authorisation and audit. Choose based on the requirement, and verify against current BPA and destination service documentation.

deep_dives.title: Two change requests, one include: a ChaRM sequencing problem
deep_dives.explanation:
The post (ref 36) describes include ZINFE0003_XXX assigned to change request 6XX0000473, while 6XX0000888 needs the same object and will be transported first. The author asks whether to remove the object and reassign it, use a separate transport, or resynchronise tracking. There is no reply.

The underlying issue is that an ABAP object is locked by one open task or request at a time. ChaRM ties transports to change requests, so moving an object by hand can desynchronise the tracking. That risk is general. The post does not give the system landscape or transport state, so I cannot say which option is safe here.

The usual options are ordering the transports so the first one carries the older version and the second builds on it, or merging both changes into one request. Reassigning after work has started is the riskiest. Before acting, check the version history of the include and the status of both transports.

This is a good example to teach, but any step-by-step advice has to be checked against the project's ChaRM configuration and SAP documentation.

interview_questions.question: You must expose files from AL11 through a RAP OData V4 service. How do you design it to prevent path traversal and unauthorised access?
interview_questions.answer: I would model the content as a stream property using a largeObject annotation and return it as Edm.Stream. The client never sends a path. It sends a logical folder key and a file name. The backend resolves the folder from a configuration table. I validate the file name against a whitelist and reject separators and '..'. After building the full path I confirm it still lies inside the mapped directory. Logical file names with FILE_VALIDATE_NAME are an option for this. I check authorisation before OPEN DATASET, and check the file size before reading it into an xstring so memory is not exhausted. Direct access to the file outside the service must also be blocked at the OS and AL11 level.

interview_questions.question: A BTP destination using OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion fails with 'Cannot determine user to propagate'. What do you check and what are your options?
interview_questions.answer: This authentication type needs a user identity to build the SAML assertion. The error means the runtime did not receive one. First I check whether the calling process runs in the user's context or in a technical context, and whether a user JWT reaches the destination lookup. The error text offers two remedies. One is to pass a user_token JWT when retrieving the destination, which keeps per-user authorisation in the target system. The other is to configure SystemUser, which uses a single identity and loses user-level audit and permissions. I choose based on the authorisation requirement. I would confirm details in the current BPA and destination service documentation, because the cause in the original post is not confirmed.

interview_questions.question: Two ChaRM change requests need changes to the same include, and the later-started one must go to production first. How do you approach it?
interview_questions.answer: I would not start by removing the object from one request and adding it to the other, because that can desynchronise ChaRM tracking from the transports. First I check the status of both requests and transports and the version history of the include. Then I look at the sequencing options. One is to release the transports in an order where the later change builds on the earlier version. Another is to merge both changes into one change request. A third is to rebase the second change on the first. The decision depends on the landscape and project ChaRM settings, so I would confirm it with the change manager and SAP documentation. The aim is that no transport overwrites a newer version of the object.
